exercises.name: Leg Extension

steps: Sit in the leg extension machine with your back against the pad and the ankle pad resting just above your feet, knees bent at 90 degrees.
Extend your legs by straightening your knees until they're fully extended, squeezing your quads at the top, then lower back down under control to the starting position.
cues: Keep the thighs supported on the seat.
Lower the shin pad without dropping the stack.
mistakes: Using too much weight often leads to using momentum — swinging the legs up quickly and letting them drop rather than controlling the movement.
Lifting the hips off the seat to help extend the legs reduces the isolation benefit of the exercise.
Locking the knees out forcefully at the top under heavy load can also place unnecessary strain on the knee joint.
structured_content.benefits: Trains knee-extension strength with the thigh supported.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: Adjust the machine to your leg length and choose a comfortable range at light resistance.

exercises.name: Leg Curl

steps: Lie face down on the leg curl machine (or sit, depending on machine type) with the ankle pad positioned just above your heels.
Curl your legs by bending your knees to bring your heels toward your glutes, squeezing your hamstrings at the top, then lower back down under control to full leg extension.
cues: Keep the hips supported as the knees bend.
Return the pad at a controlled pace.
mistakes: Lifting the hips off the pad to help curl the weight up is a very common compensation once the weight gets heavy, and it significantly reduces hamstring isolation.
Using a fast, jerky tempo rather than controlling both the lifting and lowering phases reduces the training effect.
Not achieving a full stretch at the bottom of each rep also limits range of motion benefits.
structured_content.benefits: Trains the hamstrings by bending the knee against resistance.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: Use a short controlled range initially and increase it only while the pelvis remains steady.

exercises.name: Walking Lunge

steps: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides (or bodyweight only).
Step forward with one leg and lower your body until both knees are bent at roughly 90 degrees, with your back knee hovering just above the floor.
Push through your front heel to stand up and step forward into the next lunge with the opposite leg, continuing to alternate as you walk forward.
cues: Step into a stable stance before lowering.
Alternate legs without rushing the next step.
mistakes: Letting the front knee travel excessively far forward past the toes, or letting it cave inward, are both common technique breakdowns, especially as fatigue accumulates late in a set.
Taking steps that are too short results in a narrow, unstable lunge with excessive forward knee travel.
Leaning the torso too far forward also shifts stress away from the glutes and onto the lower back.
structured_content.benefits: Builds leg strength while controlling one side of the body at a time.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: Practise a shallow bodyweight version and use a stable support if balance limits control.

exercises.name: Hip Thrust

steps: Sit on the ground with your upper back resting against a bench and a barbell positioned across your hips (padded for comfort), knees bent and feet flat on the floor about shoulder-width apart.

Drive through your heels to raise your hips up until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor and your body forms a straight line from shoulders to knees, squeezing your glutes hard at the top, then lower back down under control.
cues: Keep the upper back supported on the bench.
Finish with the hips rather than lifting the ribs.
mistakes: Hyperextending the lower back at the top of the movement rather than stopping at a straight torso-to-knee line is a very common error that shifts stress away from the glutes and onto the spine.
Not driving the hips high enough (partial range of motion) reduces the training stimulus.
Letting the knees cave inward during the drive up also reduces glute activation and stability.
structured_content.benefits: Builds hip-extension strength with the upper body supported.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: Learn to finish with the hips extended without trying to lift the ribs higher.

exercises.name: Glute Bridge

Drive through your heels to lift your hips off the ground until your body forms a straight line from shoulders to knees, squeezing your glutes at the top, then lower back down under control.
cues: Press through the feet while raising the hips.
Lower the pelvis without losing control.

structured_content.beginner_guidance: Learn to finish with the hips extended without trying to lift the ribs higher.

exercises.name: Standing Calf Raise

steps: Stand on the calf raise machine with the balls of your feet on the platform and your shoulders under the pads, heels hanging off the edge.
Lower your heels down as far as comfortable to feel a stretch in your calves, then rise up onto your toes as high as possible, squeezing at the top, before lowering back down under control.
cues: Rise through the ankles without bouncing.
Lower both heels at a steady pace.
mistakes: Using a very short range of motion — small, bouncy pulses rather than a full stretch-to-contraction range — significantly reduces the training stimulus.
Bending the knees during the movement shifts emphasis away from the gastrocnemius.
Rushing through reps without pausing at the top or bottom also reduces time under tension for this notoriously stubborn muscle group.
structured_content.benefits: Builds calf strength through controlled heel raising and lowering.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: Begin on a flat surface and use support before adding load or extra depth.

exercises.name: Plank

steps: Get into a forearm plank position with elbows directly under your shoulders and your body forming a straight line from head to heels.
Engage your core, squeeze your glutes, and hold the position, breathing steadily, without letting your hips sag or pike upward.
Hold for the prescribed time.
cues: Hold the torso steady between elbows and feet.
Keep breathing while maintaining the hold.
mistakes: Letting the hips sag toward the floor is the most common error and places excess strain on the lower back rather than the core.
Piking the hips up too high reduces the effectiveness of the exercise by taking tension off the abs.
Holding your breath instead of breathing steadily throughout the hold is another common mistake that limits how long you can maintain good form.
structured_content.benefits: Trains deliberate trunk control while the limbs or external resistance challenge position.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: Shorten the lever or movement range so you can maintain position and continue breathing.

exercises.name: Ab Wheel Roll-Out

steps: Kneel on the floor holding an ab wheel with both hands, wrists directly under shoulders.

Slowly roll the wheel forward, extending your body into as long a line as you can control while keeping your core braced and back flat, then use your abs to pull the wheel back to the starting position.
cues: Roll only as far as you can keep control.
Bring the wheel back without jerking the hips.
mistakes: Letting the lower back sag and arch as you roll out is the most common and most important error to avoid, since it shifts stress from the abs to the lower spine.
Rolling out too far too soon, before building sufficient core strength, can also lead to loss of control and potential strain.
Rushing the return phase rather than pulling back with control reduces the training benefit.

exercises.name: Rowing Machine

steps: Sit on the rowing machine with feet strapped in and grip the handle with both hands.
Drive through your legs first, then lean back slightly and pull the handle to your lower ribs, finishing with your arms bent and elbows tucked.
Reverse the sequence — extend your arms, lean forward, then bend your knees — to return to the starting position and repeat rhythmically.
cues: Move the seat and handle through a smooth stroke.
Keep the recovery controlled rather than rushing forward.
mistakes: Pulling primarily with the arms instead of driving power from the legs first is one of the most common and inefficient rowing errors.
Rounding the lower back, especially as fatigue sets in during longer intervals, can create unnecessary spinal stress.
Rushing the stroke rate without focusing on power per stroke also reduces overall efficiency and can lead to premature fatigue.
structured_content.benefits: Supports rhythmic whole-body activity at an individually chosen effort.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: Start slowly and learn the equipment controls before increasing speed or resistance.

exercises.name: Stationary Bike

steps: Adjust the seat height so your knee has a slight bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke, then sit and begin pedaling at a steady cadence.
Keep your core engaged and avoid excessive rocking of the hips, adjusting resistance and speed based on your target intensity for the session.
cues: Pedal smoothly without rocking on the saddle.
Keep a relaxed grip on the handlebars.
mistakes: An incorrect seat height — too low causes excessive knee bend and stress, too high causes hip rocking and reduced power — is one of the most common setup errors.
Gripping the handlebars too tightly and tensing the upper body wastes energy that could go toward the legs.
Pedaling with just the front of the foot rather than a fuller foot position can also reduce power efficiency.

exercises.name: Treadmill Run

steps: Start the treadmill at a comfortable walking pace to warm up, then gradually increase speed to your target running pace.
Maintain an upright posture with a slight forward lean from the ankles, land with your foot roughly under your hips rather than far out in front, and keep your arms swinging naturally at your sides.
cues: Stay centered on the moving belt.
Change speed gradually using the controls.
mistakes: Overstriding — landing with the foot far in front of the body — increases impact stress on the joints and is a very common treadmill running error, partly because the moving belt encourages it.
Holding onto the handrails while running disrupts natural arm swing and posture, and also artificially reduces the effective workload.
Starting at too fast a pace without a proper warm-up increases injury risk and often leads to early fatigue.
structured_content.benefits: Supports rhythmic whole-body activity at an individually chosen effort.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: Start slowly and learn the equipment controls before increasing speed or resistance.

exercises.name: Air Bike

steps: Sit on the air bike (fan bike) with feet on the pedals and hands gripping the moving handlebars.

Pedal and push/pull the handles simultaneously, using both your arms and legs to drive the fan, adjusting your effort level to match your target intensity — the resistance increases automatically with your effort since it's driven by a fan.

Reduce effort gradually before stopping.
mistakes: Relying mostly on the legs and barely using the arms (or vice versa) reduces the total-body benefit that makes the air bike unique.
Starting an interval at an unsustainable all-out pace without any prior conditioning can lead to early burnout or poor pacing across a workout.
Poor posture — slouching or hunching over the handlebars — can also reduce power output and cause unnecessary strain.

exercises.name: Close-Grip Bench Press

steps: Set up in a rack with safeties and use a grip around shoulder width rather than hands touching.
Lower the bar with elbows near the torso, then press back above the shoulders.
cues: Keep forearms near vertical at the bottom.
mistakes: Forcing an excessively narrow wrist position.
structured_content.benefits: Practise moving the load away from the chest while keeping a stable support position.

exercises.name: Smith Machine Bench Press

steps: Place a flat bench so the guided bar reaches the chest comfortably and set the stops.
Unhook the bar, lower toward the chest and press along the rails.
cues: Test the path with the unloaded machine.
mistakes: Positioning the bench so the bar tracks toward the neck.
structured_content.benefits: Practise moving the load away from the chest while keeping a stable support position.
